Simple enough that people understand it A compensation plan that employees cannot understand cannot influence their behavior. Complexity is not sophistication; it is a design failure. Internally equitable and legally defensible Every plan must be defensible to employees, regulators, and in litigation. There are five specific methods for dealing with conflict addressed in this program, such as: Competing, Accommodating, Avoiding, Collaborating, and Compromising. By selecting the right candidate, an organization can increase the likelihood of higher job satisfaction and reduce turnover rates. A behavioral interview is a series of open-ended questions that helps the interviewer obtain a good picture of a person’s capabilities. Good interviewing skills involve directing candidates to focus on past situations where a specific competency would have been demonstrated. To be sure that an individual has the capabilities needed to perform a job, it is important to recognize if they have demonstrated these capabilities in the past. A behavioral interview allows the interviewer to gather evidence indicating that the candidate has the critical skills and behavior required for a specific position. Compensation consulting for nonprofits requires balancing talent competition, mission-driven budgets, public disclosure, board oversight, and tax-exempt organization requirements. Nonprofits may compete with employers that pay more for similar roles while still needing compensation decisions that are explainable to employees, donors, regulators, and boards. Most nonprofits manage this tension by paying below market and hoping the mission is enough. It is not enough. The people who leave first are always those with the most options. JER HR Group’s nonprofit compensation services help organizations turn market data into practical salary ranges, executive-pay decisions, governance documentation, and implementation plans. The objective is a compensation program that is competitive enough to retain talent, structured enough for consistent administration, and documented enough for board review and applicable IRS considerations. 01 You lose your best people first High performers have options. Mission matters, but employees also evaluate whether compensation reflects the scope and market value of their work. 02 Your board faces IRS exposure IRS Section 4958 can apply when an applicable tax-exempt organization provides an excess benefit to a disqualified person. For executive compensation, boards should use an independent approval process, appropriate comparability data, and timely documentation where relevant. An organization manager can face an excise tax only under specific conditions, including knowing and willful participation in an excess benefit transaction. 03 Pay inequity quietly erodes culture When compensation is ad hoc and built through individual negotiations over many years, internal inequities accumulate silently.
